checks.Title: Seduce, don't just observe
checks.Evidence: The Three Points fair opening (bunting, fiddle, tar-and-meat smell, banners crossing ropes, soldiers sharing wine before killing each other) delivers genuine sensory seduction, but this texture is front-loaded in the first few paragraphs and then abandoned for a long stretch of procedural plot machinery — clerks, ledgers, brackets, boons, manifests — where GLMZ's strange-beautiful quality gives way to functional exposition and dialogue-heavy negotiation scenes.
checks.Fix: Thread more of that lived-in-wrong sensory texture (the graft's hum under skin, the Sinterkin's flat unhurried gaze, the construct's steam-vent rhythms) through the long middle stretch of political and financial maneuvering so allure doesn't get crowded out by mechanism.

checks.Title: Open with the world doing its work
checks.Evidence: The opening paragraphs establish Three Points as a recurring, ritualized truce-fair through grounded sensory detail (bunting left up since last time, badly-tuned fiddle, tar and roasting meat) and a toll-master who 'does not care who you are' and counts coin 'because he has' done it ten thousand times — the world functioning on its own logic before Kaeric's personal crisis (the customs board) intrudes.

checks.Title: Gloss first mentions in-voice, never dump
checks.Evidence: Terms like 'CorpoNations,' 'neuretics,' 'Catalyst infusion,' and the Sinter/Rhine geography are mostly absorbed into action without a beat of orientation (e.g., 'Sinter office... Recalculates the surcharge every fair-week' is glossed well through the clerk's dialogue), but later terms like 'Heloth courier-construct,' 'ichor-proof plate,' and 'analog' as an insult are dropped in with only partial context, assuming the reader already tracks what a construct or the Catalyst program is.
checks.Fix: Add a half-beat of in-voice sensory or functional detail the first time 'Heloth construct' and 'Catalyst infusion/program' appear (as was done well for the toll and surcharge system) so a first-time reader can place them without inferring from later exposition.

checks.Title: Never an acronym before its term
checks.Evidence: Multiple acronyms and proper nouns treated as established jargon appear without any in-voice expansion: 'NSB'-style terms aren't present, but functional equivalents like 'House Champion round,' 'Sinter office,' 'Catalyst infusion,' and especially unexplained world-terms like 'Sinterkin' and 'Sinter approach' are used as if the reader already knows the underlying system; more critically, no acronym literally appears, but the rule's spirit—never assume prior familiarity—is violated by terms like 'Catalyst' and 'Sinter' being dropped as proper nouns with capitalized specificity and no definition given anywhere in the excerpt.
checks.Fix: Introduce any specialized capitalized system-term (e.g., 'Catalyst infusion,' 'Sinter,' 'Sinterkin') with a brief in-voice gloss the first time it appears, the same way the rule demands for acronyms, so a first-time reader isn't left inferring meaning from context alone.

checks.Title: Give the POV character one human crack
checks.Evidence: "*Three days of this. Then the river again.*" followed by "Kaeric has seen it enough seasons running. It catches behind his sternum anyway" — a small, human flicker of weariness/grief at the truce-fair's temporary peace, immediately followed by him walling it back up and walking on.

checks.Title: Land one beat past the handoff
checks.Evidence: The final section does land a genuine 'one beat past' image—the field going quiet, crows and dogs working the refuse, mud 'going still' while waiting for the next truce—which is exactly the right register of weight-without-resolution. But it arrives only after an enormous cascade of unresolved plot threads (Morrint's fate, the unnamed boon, Meraq/Vaen's glove, Aeshel's debt, the freed Sinterkin) that a cold reader has no way to weigh, so the closing gesture reads as an epilogue to a sprawling saga rather than a handoff beat for this specific node.
checks.Fix: Trim the coda to focus tightly on one image tied to Kaeric/Sennah's throughline (the field, the axe, the folded paper) rather than letting it try to seal the entire multi-thread cast in one panoramic gesture.

checks.Title: Reward re-reading without requiring it
checks.Evidence: The prose does plant hindsight-rewarding details cleanly on a first pass (e.g., Kaeric's flat 'No House?'/'No' at the gate reading differently once his sister-plot and Meraq's suppressed paternity thread surface; the glove/'analog' exchange between Meraq and Vaen gains retroactive weight once Kaeric's parentage is implied), but several of these payoffs (the empty cage releasing a possible Sinterkin, the Heloth messenger scene, Morrint's ledger) are so heavily interior-monologued and thesis-stated ('That is not a threat... a man being made to carry weight he does not understand') that they explain their own significance on first read rather than leaving room to be *discovered* later — reducing the gap between first-pass and second-pass meaning.
checks.Fix: Trim the explanatory interior monologue that spells out thematic parallels (e.g., Meraq's 'That is what I have done with the name for three years' or Corrik's 'If it's true Sinterkin... that's on him') so first-time readers get the scene's surface completely while the deeper resonance is left implicit for rereaders to assemble themselves.

checks.Title: Elevate, don't reconstruct
checks.Evidence: This is not a targeted gateway pass but a sprawling, structurally dense epic spanning at least four POV threads (Kaeric, Sennah, Meraq/Vaen, Corrik) with deep lore apparatus (Catalyst infusions, Sinterkin, House politics, boons, the Long Seat, quarantine charters) delivered through dense in-world jargon with minimal orientation for a first-time reader.
checks.Fix: Cut this back to a single through-line (Kaeric/Sennah) with the other threads trimmed or removed, and add brief orienting context for terms like Sinterkin, Catalyst infusion, and the Houses so a newcomer isn't relying on accumulated lore to track stakes.
